paragraphImitation.directions: Study the model paragraph (¶1–2) and its Paragraph Logic chain from Text Walkthrough. Choose ONE transferable scenario, then write a new English paragraph that follows the same development: Open claim → Turn: half the picture → Old assumption → Radical idea → Stakes.
paragraphImitation.sourceTitle: The Puzzle and the Radical Idea
paragraphImitation.modelParagraph: Memory makes us who we are. For more than a century, researchers have worked to understand how memories are formed and then fixed for recall. But those scientists might have been looking at only half the picture. To understand how we remember, we must also understand how, and why, we forget. Until about ten years ago, most researchers thought that forgetting was a passive process in which memories, unused, decay over time like a photograph left in the sunlight. Then a handful of researchers investigating memory began to bump up against findings that seemed to contradict that decades-old assumption, and they began to put forward the radical idea that the brain is built to forget. A growing body of work suggests that the loss of memories is not a passive process. Rather, forgetting seems to be an active mechanism, constantly at work in the brain; in some animals, the brain's standard state is not to remember, but to forget. A better understanding of this state could lead to breakthroughs in treatments for anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, and even Alzheimer's disease.
